body:
Why are nanomaterials useful?

Nanotechnology is useful because scientists and manufacturers can sometimes obtain properties that are difficult to achieve using conventional bulk materials.

The practical advantage depends on the particular material. A large accessible surface may improve catalysis or sensing. A controlled electronic structure may produce useful optical effects. A thin nanoscale coating may improve the performance of a much larger object.

The important relationship is therefore nanoscale structure, resulting property and practical application.

1. Sunscreens and ultraviolet protection

Ultraviolet (UV) radiation from sunlight can damage the skin. Sunscreens protect the skin by reducing the amount of harmful UV radiation reaching it.

Zinc oxide (ZnO) and titanium dioxide (TiO2) are mineral ingredients used in some sunscreens. They interact with ultraviolet radiation through absorption and scattering.

When suitably formulated with nanoscale particles, these ingredients can provide UV protection while creating less visible white residue than some formulations containing larger mineral particles.

However, the effectiveness and safety of a sunscreen depend on its complete formulation, testing and intended use. Nanoscale particles alone do not guarantee better sun protection.

2. Water purification and environmental protection

Water purification requires the removal or reduction of unwanted particles, microorganisms or dissolved contaminants, depending on the water source.

Some nanostructured materials are useful because they provide large accessible surfaces, selective interactions with contaminants or extremely small structures that can contribute to separation processes.

Examples include:

  • Nanostructured adsorbents: Materials designed to bind selected contaminants to their surfaces.
  • Nanostructured membranes: Membrane materials whose nanoscale features may help control the passage of water and selected substances.
  • Specialised catalysts: Materials that can assist certain chemical processes used in pollution treatment.

The effectiveness of a water-treatment system depends on the contaminant, material, filtration method and maintenance. A filter is not automatically capable of producing safe drinking water merely because it contains a nanomaterial.

3. Catalysts in vehicles and industries

Many industrial chemical reactions require catalysts to proceed at useful rates. Solid catalysts act through interactions occurring on their surfaces.

Reducing an appropriate catalytic material to nanoscale particles can expose more surface sites per unit mass. This may improve catalytic performance or reduce the amount of expensive material required.

In automotive catalytic converters, catalytic materials help transform harmful exhaust pollutants into less harmful substances. Nanostructured catalysts are also useful in selected industrial chemical processes.

The key property is accessible catalytic surface, not particle size alone.

4. Sensors and detection

A sensor detects a physical, chemical or biological change and produces a measurable response.

Nanomaterials may help sensors detect small quantities of certain substances because many surface atoms are available to interact with the surrounding environment.

When a target substance attaches to a suitable sensing surface, it may change an electrical or optical signal. The sensor then uses that change for detection.

Potential and established applications across different technologies include gas sensors, environmental monitoring and selected medical diagnostic devices.

Each sensor must be designed for the particular substance or property it is intended to detect. A large surface area does not automatically make a sensor selective.

5. Electronics and displays

Nanotechnology allows some electronic components and materials to be produced with extremely small dimensions. Such structures can support compact devices and new electrical or optical functions.

Quantum dots are used in certain display technologies because they can produce selected colours of light. Their size-dependent light emission helps manufacturers obtain particular optical characteristics.

Other nanomaterials, including selected thin films and carbon-based structures, are used or investigated for electronic components, conducting coatings and flexible devices.

However, an electronic product being small does not automatically mean that all its components are nanomaterials. The relevant material or feature must have nanoscale dimensions.

6. Medicine and drug delivery

Nanoparticles and other nanoscale carriers are used or investigated in medicine because their size and surface properties can be controlled to influence how they interact with biological systems.

Some nanotechnology-based formulations can help transport medicines or modify how particular drugs are released or distributed.

Such behaviour depends on the material's composition, size, surface properties and the medicine being carried. Nanoparticles do not automatically travel to a diseased organ or selectively destroy unhealthy cells.

Medical applications require evidence of effectiveness and safety for the specific formulation.

7. Stronger materials and protective coatings

Nanoscale additives can modify the mechanical properties of plastics, coatings and other composite materials.

A composite material combines different materials to obtain a useful set of properties. Properly incorporated nanoscale fillers may improve selected properties such as stiffness, strength or wear resistance.

Nanostructured surface coatings can also provide properties such as improved resistance to scratching, corrosion or contamination, depending on their composition and design.

8. Batteries and energy technologies

Batteries store and release energy through electrochemical reactions. The structure and properties of their electrode materials influence how efficiently these reactions occur.

Nanostructured electrode materials can provide greater accessible surface area and shorter distances for movement of ions within selected structures. These features may improve some aspects of charging or power delivery.

They can also create challenges, including unwanted surface reactions and reduced long-term stability. Thus, making an electrode material smaller does not guarantee a better battery.

Relating nanoscale properties to uses

Useful propertyRepresentative application
Controlled interaction with UV and visible lightMineral sunscreens
Large accessible surface for selected contaminantsWater-treatment adsorbents
Large accessible catalytic surfaceAutomotive and industrial catalysts
Surface-sensitive electrical or optical responseChemical and biological sensors
Size-dependent light emissionQuantum-dot displays
Controlled particle or surface propertiesSelected drug-delivery systems
Modified mechanical propertiesComposite materials and protective coatings
Controlled electrode structure and surface areaSelected battery technologies

These examples show that nanotechnology is not restricted to a single industry. Its uses arise from different physical and chemical properties, and the relevant mechanism must be identified separately in each case.

Prelims focus

  • Zinc oxide and titanium dioxide are mineral ingredients used in certain sunscreens.
  • Nanostructured adsorbents can bind selected contaminants at their surfaces.
  • Large accessible surface area can improve the performance of suitable catalysts.
  • Quantum dots can provide selected colours of light in displays.
  • Nanoscale materials are used or studied in sensors, medicine, coatings and energy technologies.
  • Trap: A potential use of a nanomaterial is not proof that every product containing it is effective or safe.

[Sources: National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'Applications of Nanotechnology', sections 'Everyday Materials and Processes', 'Electronics and IT Applications', 'Medical and Healthcare Applications' and 'Energy Applications', accessed 13 November 2026; National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, 'Nanomaterials', section 'What are nanomaterials?', accessed 13 November 2026; National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'What Is So Special About Nano?', sections on surface and quantum effects, accessed 13 November 2026.]
title: Applications of Nanotechnology: Connecting Properties with Practical Uses

body:
Does smaller always mean better?

Reducing the dimensions of a material can produce useful changes, but small size is not automatically an advantage.

Several factors influence the properties of a nanomaterial:

  • Composition: The atoms and chemical compounds from which the material is made.
  • Size: The dimensions of the particles or structures.
  • Shape: Whether the material forms particles, tubes, wires, sheets or another structure.
  • Surface characteristics: The chemical nature of the exposed surfaces and any substances attached to them.
  • Arrangement: Whether particles are separated, grouped into clusters or incorporated into another material.
  • Surrounding conditions: The liquid, gas, temperature or other environment in which the material is used.

Two materials with the same average particle size need not exhibit the same behaviour. Even samples of the same substance may differ if their shapes or surface characteristics are different.

What problems can arise from nanoscale dimensions?

Particle clustering

Nanoparticles may associate into clusters or agglomerates. When this happens, some of their surfaces become less accessible, reducing the expected benefits of high surface area.

Unwanted chemical reactions

A large exposed surface can be useful for catalysis, but it can also allow unwanted reactions with the surrounding environment. In some applications, such reactions reduce the stability or useful life of a material.

Changes during use

A nanomaterial may change as it is exposed to air, water, heat or other substances. Some particles may dissolve, change their surfaces, become attached to other materials or form larger clusters.

The behaviour of the material in a finished product therefore may differ from that of isolated particles studied separately.

Nanomaterials and health or environmental safety

Nanomaterials can interact with living organisms and the environment in ways that differ from some larger forms of the same substances.

Possible exposure routes include inhalation of airborne particles, ingestion and contact with the skin. The significance of an exposure depends on the specific material and its circumstances.

Safety assessment must consider:

  • The material's composition and particle size.
  • Its shape and surface chemistry.
  • The amount and duration of exposure.
  • The route through which exposure occurs.
  • Whether particles are freely dispersed or securely contained within another material.
  • What happens to the material during use and after disposal.

For example, exposure to a freely dispersed nanoparticle powder differs from contact with a solid product containing particles securely embedded in its structure. The actual risk must be assessed for the particular material and exposure conditions.

Hazard is not the same as risk

A hazard is the potential of a substance or situation to cause harm. Risk concerns the likelihood and seriousness of harm under particular exposure conditions.

Neither the statement that all nanomaterials are dangerous nor the statement that all nanomaterials are harmless is scientifically justified.

Nanoscale materials occur in nature as well as in engineered products

Nanoscale particles and structures are not always manufactured by humans. Natural processes can also produce materials with nanoscale dimensions.

Nanotechnology generally refers to deliberate understanding and control of matter at this scale to obtain useful results. Thus, naturally occurring nanoscale matter and engineered nanomaterials should be distinguished.

A further distinction concerns everyday molecules. The fact that an individual molecule is extremely small does not automatically mean that a product containing it is a nanotechnology product. The relevant nanoscale structure, phenomenon or controlled application must be considered.

Nanoscience and nanotechnology in India

India has supported research in nanoscience and nanotechnology through national scientific institutions, universities and government research programmes.

National Nano Mission

The Department of Science and Technology (DST), Government of India, launched the Nano Mission in 2007 as a national capacity-building programme for nanoscience and nanotechnology.

Its major objectives included promoting basic research, developing research infrastructure, supporting technological applications, developing skilled human resources and encouraging international scientific collaboration.

The original programme covered 2007–2012 and was extended for a second phase covering 2012–2017.

Following the second phase, the programme was converted into the National Programme on Nano Science and Technology (NPNST) in 2017.

The DST Annual Report for 2024–25 describes related work under the Nano and Advanced Materials Divisions (NAMD) and records a call for advanced-materials research proposals during September–October 2024.

These are historical and 2024–25 reporting facts, rather than a claim that the original 2007 Nano Mission continued accepting new projects under the same arrangements at the 13 November 2026 content cutoff.

Gujarat connection: Research at IIT Gandhinagar

Indian Institute of Technology Gandhinagar (IIT Gandhinagar), located in Gujarat, includes nanomaterials among the research areas of its Materials Engineering department.

Its published research areas also include thin films, transparent conducting oxides, solar cells and related materials technologies.

The institute's research facilities include instruments used to examine and characterise materials at very small scales.

This provides an example of nanomaterials research within Gujarat's higher-education and scientific research ecosystem. It should not be confused with the national Nano Mission or treated as evidence of a separate Gujarat government nanotechnology programme.

Putting the whole concept together

The conventional nanoscale of approximately 1–100 nm is important because size can strongly influence material behaviour. Two especially important explanations are the increased influence of surfaces and the appearance of quantum-size effects in suitable structures.

When the surface-area-to-volume ratio increases, more of the material is accessible for interactions with surrounding substances. This can influence catalysis, adsorption and certain chemical reactions. Quantum confinement in suitable semiconductor structures can change electronic energy states and the wavelengths of absorbed or emitted light.

Other changes in optical, electrical, thermal, magnetic or mechanical properties depend on the material's composition and structure. These differences help explain the use of nanomaterials in catalysts, filters, sunscreens, sensors, displays, coatings and selected medical or energy technologies.

Yet useful performance depends on more than particle size. The material's shape, stability, surface characteristics, exposure conditions and safety must also be considered.

Prelims focus

  • The main causes of unusual nanoscale behaviour include surface-area effects and quantum-size effects.
  • Nanomaterial properties depend on composition, size, shape, surfaces and surrounding conditions.
  • Nanoparticle clustering can reduce accessible surface area.
  • Hazard describes potential harm; risk also depends on exposure conditions.
  • India's Nano Mission was launched by DST in 2007 and transitioned into NPNST in 2017.
  • IIT Gandhinagar is an example of an institution conducting nanomaterials research in Gujarat.
  • Trap: The benefits or risks of one nanomaterial must not automatically be attributed to all nanomaterials.

[Sources: National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, 'Nanomaterials', sections 'What are nanomaterials?' and 'What are some of the main take-home points?', accessed 13 November 2026; National Institute of Environmental Health Sciences, 'Nano Environmental Health and Safety', programme description, accessed 13 November 2026; Department of Science and Technology, Government of India, Annual Report 2024–25, section 2.3, 'Nano and Advanced Materials Divisions', printed p. 58; Department of Science and Technology, 'Nano India highlights India efforts in nurturing nano-science excellence', historical programme account, published 2020; IIT Gandhinagar, 'Materials Engineering', research areas and facilities, accessed 13 November 2026; National Nanotechnology Coordination Office, 'About Nanotechnology', 'What Is So Special About Nano?' and 'Applications of Nanotechnology', accessed 13 November 2026.]
